subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Overuse injuries of the elbow and wrist
vignette: A 42-year-old man who recently increased his golf practice reports 3 weeks of aching pain along the inner aspect of his right elbow. The pain is reproduced by gripping a club and by resisted wrist flexion. There is focal tenderness just distal to the medial epicondyle without swelling or neurodeficits.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)
Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)
Ulnar collateral ligament rupture
Olecranon bursitis
Cubital tunnel syndrome

explanation_correct: Medial (golfer's) elbow tendinopathy results from repetitive wrist flexion or idiopathic stress and produces pain near the medial epicondyle. This patient's pain with gripping and resisted wrist flexion, with focal medial epicondylar tenderness, is classic. Lateral epicondylitis would be painful over the lateral epicondyle with wrist extension instead.

explanation_incorrect.A: Lateral epicondylitis causes pain near the lateral epicondyle and is provoked by wrist extension, not the medial tenderness and flexion pain described here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Ulnar collateral ligament rupture usually follows an acute valgus injury with instability, not insidious overuse with point tenderness at the epicondyle.
explanation_incorrect.D: Olecranon bursitis produces a fluctuant swelling over the posterior olecranon rather than focal medial epicondylar tenderness with resisted wrist flexion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cubital tunnel syndrome compresses the ulnar nerve at the elbow and causes paresthesias in the fifth and medial fourth fingers, not localized tendinopathy pain.

educationalObjective: Medial (golfer's) elbow is tendinopathy from repetitive wrist flexion causing pain at the medial epicondyle.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Overuse injuries of the elbow and wrist
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has 6 weeks of outer elbow pain that began after repeated backhand strokes at tennis. Tenderness is maximal over the lateral epicondyle, and pain is elicited by resisted wrist extension. She has no numbness or nighttime pain.
question: Which structure is most likely affected?

options.text: Common flexor tendon origin at the medial epicondyle
Ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel
Extensor tendons at the lateral epicondyle
Articular cartilage of the radial head
Distal biceps tendon insertion

explanation_correct: Lateral (tennis) elbow tendinopathy is caused by repetitive wrist extension, classically backhand shots, and produces pain near the lateral epicondyle where the extensor tendons originate. Resisted wrist extension reproduces the pain. The corresponding medial injury involves the flexor tendons and is provoked by wrist flexion.

explanation_incorrect.A: The common flexor origin at the medial epicondyle is involved in medial (golfer's) elbow from repetitive wrist flexion, not lateral elbow pain with extension.
explanation_incorrect.B: The ulnar nerve in the cubital tunnel produces sensory loss and tingling in ulnar-distribution fingers, not isolated lateral epicondylar tenderness.
explanation_incorrect.D: Radial head articular cartilage injury would cause intra-articular pain and mechanical symptoms rather than focal epicondylar tenderness with resisted wrist extension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Distal biceps tendon pathology causes anterior elbow pain and weakness of supination and flexion, not lateral epicondylar pain with wrist extension.

educationalObjective: Lateral (tennis) elbow is extensor tendinopathy at the lateral epicondyle caused by repetitive wrist extension.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Overuse injuries of the elbow and wrist
vignette: A 29-year-old manual laborer has medial elbow soreness after weeks of repetitive hammering, which requires forceful wrist flexion. Physical examination shows tenderness over the medial epicondyle and pain when the examiner resists wrist flexion with the forearm pronated.
question: Which maneuver is most likely to reproduce this patient's pain?

options.text: Resisted wrist extension
Passive finger extension with the wrist neutral
Resisted forearm supination with the elbow flexed
Resisted wrist flexion
Passive elbow extension with the wrist flexed

explanation_correct: Medial epicondylitis is a tendinopathy of the wrist flexor origin caused by repetitive wrist flexion. Because the pathology is at the common flexor tendon origin, resisted wrist flexion reproduces the pain at the medial epicondyle. This distinguishes it from lateral epicondylitis, in which resisted wrist extension is painful.

explanation_incorrect.A: Resisted wrist extension stresses the lateral extensor origin and would reproduce lateral (tennis) elbow pain, not medial tendinopathy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Passive finger extension stretches the flexors but is not the standard provocative maneuver and would not selectively load the medial epicondyle as resisted flexion does.
explanation_incorrect.C: Resisted forearm supination primarily stresses the biceps tendon and is not the classic test for medial epicondylar tendinopathy.
explanation_incorrect.E: Passive elbow extension with the wrist flexed stretches the flexor mass but is not the resisted maneuver that reliably reproduces medial epicondylitis pain.

educationalObjective: Medial epicondylitis pain is reproduced by resisted wrist flexion, whereas lateral epicondylitis pain is reproduced by wrist extension.

subject: Musculoskeletal
subtopic: Overuse injuries of the elbow and wrist
vignette: Two patients present with elbow pain from overuse. The first has tenderness over the lateral epicondyle brought on by backhand tennis strokes; the second has medial epicondylar tenderness brought on by repetitive wrist flexion. A medical student is asked to state the key mechanical distinction between the two conditions.
question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes lateral from medial epicondylitis?

options.text: Lateral epicondylitis is caused by repetitive wrist flexion
Medial epicondylitis is classically triggered by backhand wrist extension
Medial epicondylitis produces tenderness over the lateral epicondyle
Lateral epicondylitis typically involves compression of the ulnar nerve
Lateral epicondylitis results from repetitive wrist extension; medial from repetitive wrist flexion

explanation_correct: The two epicondylitides are distinguished by location and by the direction of the repetitive wrist motion that provokes them. Lateral (tennis) elbow is extensor tendinopathy from repetitive wrist extension such as backhand shots and is tender over the lateral epicondyle. Medial (golfer's) elbow is flexor tendinopathy from repetitive wrist flexion and is tender over the medial epicondyle.

explanation_incorrect.A: Repetitive wrist flexion causes medial, not lateral, epicondylitis; the lateral side is stressed by extension.
explanation_incorrect.B: Backhand wrist extension is the classic trigger for lateral tennis elbow, not medial golfer's elbow.
explanation_incorrect.C: By definition medial epicondylitis is tender at the medial epicondyle; lateral tenderness indicates lateral epicondylitis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Ulnar nerve compression at the elbow is cubital tunnel syndrome, not lateral epicondylitis, which is a tendon disorder.

educationalObjective: Lateral epicondylitis follows repetitive wrist extension and medial epicondylitis follows repetitive wrist flexion, with tenderness at the corresponding epicondyle.
